utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good morning to everyone. The Chamber regrets that it was not able to deliver the decision on postponement of Mr. Deronjic's examination, but hopes to deliver that this morning. Since my LiveNote is not yet awake, I'll try to ... My computer as a whole doesn't want to start up. But let's get started. Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Deronjic to the courtroom. Yes, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, before Mr. Deronjic comes into Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I straight away deal with this matter, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Defence does ask for a break, a relatively short break, between the completion of Mr. Deronjic's evidence in chief and cross-examination. Without elaborating, Your Honour knows very well the general pressures that everybody, but certainly the Defence team, have been under in relation to the early stages of this trial. But so far as Mr. Deronjic is concerned -- and Your Honour, I make it plain straight away what I'm asking for. I'm not asking for some enormously long break. We're actually going to propose two possibilities. One is that on the footing that we rather think from discussions with Mr. Harmon that it looks as if Mr. Deronjic's evidence in chief will come to an end sometime late today. That seemed to be the rough estimate. Of course, that's entirely in Mr. Harmon's and the Tribunal's hands, but unless the position has changed, that seemed to be broadly the position. On the footing that that's what's pretty much going to happen, we would ask, as, if you like, alternative one, that the Tribunal should not sit tomorrow, that we should resume on Wednesday. That would give us that 36-hour or so opportunity to -- well, to further work on Mr. Deronjic. The alternative, and we only suggest this as an alternative in case it were to work better for everybody, is that we understand that Mr. Treanor could be available, or that was the position last week anyway, that Mr. Treanor could be available to give his evidence in chief at relatively short notice. It would be possible to deal with him and then come back to Mr. Deronjic in this two-week period. Because it's understood that on no footing are we going to be cross-examining Mr. Treanor anyway before the break and until after Easter. So we just suggest that as an alternative. The first possibility, that we -- the advantage of the second alternative, Your Honour, is that that may have the effect of losing no court time at all this week. Though the practical effect may very well be the same anyway, because in this 18-day period it looks as if, despite some of Your Honour's expressed concerns about timing, it looks as if in fact we're making pretty good progress and we will finish off the chunk of evidence that everybody had in mind within this 18-day period, and we might end up with a little bit of time to spare at the end which won't, in a sense, be bad news. That will have been that we will have completed the programme of evidence that was contemplated within that 18-day period. But, Your Honour, in an absolute nutshell, without laying bare all the difficulties and the pressures on the Defence team, if I can just give one or two simple illustrations. Mr. Deronjic gave -- was cross-examined for four days in the Blagojevic case between the 19th and the 22nd, I think it was, of January, which was about ten days before the trial started. So we have four days of his cross-examination, which comes upon us in transcript form. And of course there's a delay before the -- am I going too fast? I'm not sure, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not for me, but perhaps for the interpreters and the court reporter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Apparently I'm not. I am -- the light is shining on the --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: You are going too fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll slow down a little bit, Your Honour, then. So we have those four days of transcript cross-examination, which became officially available, I think actually after this trial started. We also have important new areas of evidence of Mr. Deronjic. I don't exaggerate by suggesting that tremendously voluminous in content but they are very important in substance, the additional areas which are highlighted in the amended witness summary. I don't wish to exaggerate that, but they are important areas. And from a practical point of view, I know that Your Honours will understand that although all sorts of advantages in sitting in the morning last week, sitting in the morning does create great difficulties in finding time with Mr. Krajisnik, because the earliest we're able to get to the Detention Unit for practical purposes is 3.00. We then have an hour and three quarters with a client who has, after all, been in court all day for five hours, leaving aside the fact that the legal team are only human, but we're deemed to be superhuman in that area, but the client can't be deemed to be that in the same way. So that there is tremendous pressure in achieving sufficient time and effective communication with the client in connection with these important aspects. The same would apply today in the -- when the court sits in the afternoon it is a little easier because we can get a couple of hours first thing in the morning. But Your Honour is, I think, very familiar with those pressures, and we have reviewed the position this morning. We decided to soldier on over the weekend and see where we were, but we have all compared notes, the Defence team this morning on this matter, and though reluctant to take this step and genuinely, Your Honour, because we have -- I think you can see that we have tried very hard to keep up with the programme and we have not sought any respite over the last couple of weeks. We have cracked on through these witnesses and we have dealt with the programme. But we are really very stretched here, Your Honour, and in fairness to Mr. Krajisnik and in order to be able to collate the very voluminous material -- there are hundreds and hundreds of pages of interviews of Mr. Deronjic. I don't suggest we haven't had those for quite a long time but that's not entirely the point. We do have to put them together with all the other material in the light of Mr. Deronjic's examination-in-chief. Your Honour, I could go -- I could go on and on about the practical difficulties, but I believe that Your Honour is well aware of the -- has a good feel of the overall practical situation. That one day and we suggest it probably won't be lost in any serious sense because we -- it looks as if we will complete the programme of evidence that we had in mind during this 18-day period anyway. But for the Court not to sit for those four or five hours tomorrow will give us a clear run through from early this afternoon until Wednesday afternoon, and that will be invaluable in terms of simply reviewing the position, collating the material, achieving some proper time with our own client in advance of beginning Mr. Deronjic's cross-examination. With the added point, without being able, perhaps, to make it as a big promise, but Your Honours will also know that a little bit of extra preparation time can actually hone down and refine the cross-examination a bit so that time gets saved anyway, that a little bit less preparation time sometimes adds a bit of time to cross-examination. Whereas if it can be a little bit more efficiently honed then you save time ultimately anyway. So Your Honour, that is our application, that the Court does not sit tomorrow. This is -- if the programme of Mr. Deronjic's examination-in-chief changes radically, that would be a different matter, but I don't -- I don't understand that there's any significant departure from where we understood we were on Friday, which is that Mr. Deronjic's examination-in-chief is likely to take all or most of today but not very different from all or most of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you say might even be a good investment. Mr. Harmon, if we would not sit tomorrow -- well, things do not change considerably for the Prosecution. If you would start the examination-in-chief of Mr. Treanor that, of course, would at least change the order of presentation of your evidence and the cross-examination of Mr. Deronjic. The Chamber would like -- not necessarily right away, but would like to hear the position from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel. Our position is this: Mr. Deronjic was identified as a witness on the 22nd of October of this year. On the 12th of December -- of last year? On the 12th of December, he was identified in order of when he would be called. Production of statements to the Defence was completed a considerable period ago. In respect of calling Mr Treanor at this point in time, that would not be possible because we are in the process of organising and preparing his exhibits. He has voluminous exhibits and it's not possible for us to start with Mr Treanor. In respect of adjourning a day, I submit that's -- we have -- we're neutral on that, Your Honour, and I would leave that to the Trial Chamber to decide the best manner in which to proceed in this case. But in respect of the second suggestion by counsel, we are opposed to it. We simply couldn't be ready.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would it be possible for the parties to inform the Chamber a bit more in detail, that is, I would say a scheme on what days we'll hear what evidence if we would not sit for one day, so that we are quite clear that we would fulfil the programme we had in mind for the first 18 days. I'll ask the -- so that the Chamber can be confident that a delay of one day would not really disturb our time scheduling. I'll ask the registrar also to provide the Chamber with the full statistics on what happened over the last few days and we'll consider it, but we'd like very much the parties to sit together and say: Okay. If we have one day for break, we expect the cross-examination to take so much time. Because we're not informed yet about that, and the programme then would be so-and-so. So that we get a time -- a kind of a time path for the two weeks to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll just comment. Two comments, Your Honour. One is of course I accept unreservedly if the Prosecution say -- it's rather what we're saying in relation to Mr. Deronjic. If the Prosecution say they can't be ready for Mr. Treanor at this stage we accept that completely. We express surprise because last week when Your Honour asked the Prosecution specifically whether Mr. Treanor could be ready for the following day the answer was yes, he could. So if he could be ready the following day last week, that information at the time must have been overconfident. So it seems to have been superseded. Our second comment is only that part of the programme that Your Honour has asked for, and we endorse with respect that request entirely, concerns the position of Mr. Hasanovic, whose travel arrangements were in doubt. So the earlier that the Prosecution are able -- it's pretty early in the United States at the moment, but the earlier the Prosecution are able to explore the position -- current position of Mr. Hasanovic, the better we shall be able to refine the projected timetable for the next ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We continue to monitor the travel situation of Mr. Hasanovic, and as soon as I have information I will make Your Honours aware of it and I will advise counsel of it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, so we'll consider your request, Mr. Stewart, and I add to that that the time when it was indicated that Mr. Deronjic would testify and the time that the statements were given of course does not solve the problem of his cross-examination. The case is still to be studied by the Defence. And to that extent, I would agree that if you can go through cross-examination of -- in the other cases, then of course this could, although not necessarily does save time. Then having dealt with this, Mr. Usher, could you please escort Mr. Deronjic into the courtroom. I'd like to add to that that the Chamber appreciates that both parties are, in our view, at least, trying to do their utmost to work as efficiently as possible, but it is as in sport, we always can do better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Deronjic said "dobro jutro."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Good morning, Your Excellency. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Deronjic, please be seated. May I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration that you've given at the beginning of your testimony, and may I also remind you to my words that I spoke at the beginning of your testimony about your obligation to testify in accordance with the truth and that no reason whatsoever could justify any deviation, small or large, from that truth. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If Mr. Deronjic could be provided with the two notebooks that he had before him, as well as Prosecutor's Exhibit 51, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, when we concluded the examination on Friday, we were discussing an evaluation report by General Kukanjac, whose zone of responsibility was the 2nd Military District. This report is dated the 3rd of -- March the 20th of 1992. And I was directing your attention to certain elements in that report that are found under the heading number 5: "Volunteer units in the zone of the 2nd Military District." And I would direct your attention to that page. Can you find it in the report in front of you, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We were talking about the arming of the Bosnian Serbs by the JNA, and I'd like to direct your attention to subpart (F), 5(F), and invite your comments on that. This is the part that reads: "JNA distributed 51.900 pieces of armament (75 per cent) and SDS 17.298 pieces." I invite your comments on that, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my previous statements, I said that Serbs from the beginning of 1991, from the spring of 1991, began to arm themselves and that they used several sources for these weapons, amongst them the JNA also was involved in this arming. From this report, you can see that the JNA here gave a figure. The number of pieces that were distributed to Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina, or in this army zone. And this is 50.500 pieces, and you can clearly see that the SDS participated in this, or some people from the SDS were also involved in this arming, which I discussed before. And the number of weapons distributed by the SDS up to that moment amounted to 17.296 pieces. So this is my interpretation of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Just to correct the record, it says on line 3, 50.500 pieces. How many pieces did the JNA distribute?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here: "Distributed 51.900 pieces."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, this report, Mr. Deronjic, deals with the 2nd Military District. I direct your attention to subpart 5(E), which references the 4th Military District, another military district of the JNA. And could you read that portion? And I'm particularly interested in the part of that -- subpart (E) that is in parenthesis, that reads: "That was formed earlier by the 4th Corps."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've read that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you have any comments in respect of that paragraph, Mr. Deronjic, particularly in respect of whether -- the observation in this paragraph that indicates that the volunteer units were formed by the 4th Corps of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I can interpret this in the light of events which were taking place in 1991 and 1992. The fact that the military went through various transformations are well known, that it adapted its composition to the circumstances in the field. I know that already in January 1991, there was a series of transformations of the Yugoslav People's Army, in the sense of changing the military districts and the jurisdictions of the military units in certain districts, and all of this was conditioned by these broader political developments. Also a well-known fact is that the members of the other two ethnic groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not respond to the summonses by the JNA, and this forming and manning of the JNA, the replenishment, was conducted on the basis of volunteers or those who did respond to the call-up. However, I don't have any particular information about this, and I wasn't involved in this. But anyway, it was basically done through the volunteers who reported to these units. That's what I am understanding from this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, I'd like to direct your attention to the portion of the report, the caption above which is "some experiences." It may be on the same page. It follows letter G. And I'd like to direct your attention to what is in the English translation, the second paragraph. It reads: "Certain leaders in SDS on all levels are using different channels to demand the weapons from JNA and Serbia, and in that way, they fight for the predominance, that is, creating the dissatisfaction in people and dividing them." Can you provide some comments in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. It is true that during 1991, certain individuals -- actually, a large number of them, including myself -- were involved in the arming of Serbs. This particular paragraph concerns the fact that people were exerting pressure on the JNA to arm Serbs, and to the extent I had an opportunity to see from various documents, I know that they were actually in the field, on the ground, and that the weapons were reaching the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this report that is before you, General Kukanjac's report, Mr. Deronjic, when was the first time you saw this report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this report for the first time five or six days ago, when you showed it to me, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And prior to that, you had given the Office of the Prosecutor extensive information in respect of the arming of the Serbs; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, based on your knowledge of the events, your personal role in arming efforts of the Serbs, can you tell me,

utterances.speaker: MR. DERONJIC
utterances.text: Why was it that the Serbs were being armed?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me. Could you please repeat your question? I pressed a button to lower the volume and I just didn't hear you for a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you hear me now, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is the volume all right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to test. So is it all right, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it will be okay now. 5 Q. My question is, Mr. Deronjic: Based on your personal involvement in the 6 arming of the Bosnian Serbs and your contacts with other people in respect of 7 that same issue, why was it that the Bosnian Serbs were arming themselves? 8 A. Yes. I understand your question. I have to say that, as far as the stage 9 in which I was involved with arming is concerned, Yugoslavia was exposed to 10 a lot of danger. We were aware of a number of affairs involving the arming of other people, especially in Croatia. At that time, the affair involving 12 Mr. Spegelj in the arming of the Croats in Croatia was already a matter of 13 public knowledge. This was also broadcast by the electronic media at the 14 time. To what extent this information was accurate, I don't know. All I 15 know about it was from the knowledge I had from the media. But I have to 16 draw your attention to the fact that people still remembered very tragic 17 events from the Second World War. Of course, I'm not trying to say that 18 only Serbs were the victims during that war. Everybody was a victim, and 19 this is a matter of historical record. But I have to say that everybody 20 was afraid of a potential conflict, including members of other ethnic 21 communities, and so far as I know, others were arming themselves as well, and 22 I am quite confident about that 23 It is true that the Serbs were arming themselves because they were fearful of the possibility that during the breakup of Yugoslavia, during the crisis in Yugoslavia, certain things which had happened in the past could happen again. And I am convinced that this fear was the reason for the people to arm themselves, and they were of course under a lot of pressure to do that. And this is -- this, I think, would be the reason for their arming. I may have not interpreted the best way I could, but this crisis in Yugoslavia contributed to a large extent to this atmosphere of fear in Yugoslavia. And then again, there was the pressure on the people, because they did not fully trust the Yugoslav People's Army, and because of its multi-ethnic character, and because of its nature, generally speaking, it was an ideological army, after all, they did not know how the military would behave in this breakup. Those would be the reasons that I was able to identify during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, you were involved in the arming efforts in April, as I recall your testimony, in April and the early part of 1991. From the report that is before you, Mr. Deronjic, the army efforts continued. This report is dated the 20th of March, 1992. Do you have a view as to why the army efforts continued and with the intensity that they did, after April of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have a view on that. As I have already indicated, the crisis in Yugoslavia, in particular, the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina, had entered its final dramatic stage in the autumn of 1991 and the beginning of 1992. This was the period when Republika Srpska was being established, and it was a public thing. Its institutions were being founded at that time. I have already spoken about the fact that the JNA at that time already favoured Serbs and supported their plans, and this arming of the Serbs can be directly linked to that, to the formation of Republika Srpska. And, well, it is my assumption that there was a lot of military activity going on with regard to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Deronjic, thank you very much. I've concluded with Prosecutor's Exhibit 51. I'd like to turn to another exhibit, Mr. Deronjic, and that is -- the next in order --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have a number for that exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P52.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And before this exhibit is shown to -- you can take it up and just hold on to it for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, on Friday, I believe, you indicated in your testimony that a man by the name of Rajko Dukic, you believed, was an important figure in the financing of the SDS, and you heard it as a rumour -- this was a rumour. I'd like to put before you this exhibit. Have you ever seen this exhibit before, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Dukic, in your previous testimony, you mentioned that he was, I believe, the owner of the bauxite mine, an important commercial concern in Bosnia, and he was also a member of the Executive Board of the SDS and one of its founders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But let me correct the interpreters. It is not Mr. Djukic, but Mr. Dukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I think that's a result of my poor pronunciation. I apologise, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you, Mr. Harmon. I see that attachment to P52 are in a language which is not an official language of the Tribunal. Does that cause the Defence any problem? I see it's in German.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document, for the record, Your Honour, I provided to the Defence on Friday evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm informed about that. But it's perhaps mainly on that basis that having been informed that it has been disclosed only lately. I know some German, so if --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, so does the Defence team, actually, Your Honour, so that just slightly softens the blow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I direct your attention -- first of all, this document is dated the 15th of December, 1992, and it is addressed to President Karadzic, and a copy of which is sent to Mr. Krajisnik, the Assembly president. And I direct your attention, Mr. Deronjic, to the first two paragraphs of this document. And Mr. Deronjic, is this consistent with the rumour that you had heard that Mr. Dukic was one of the financiers of the party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. We can see clearly from this that payments were being made, such as this last one, a hundred thousand German marks. The report concerns this particular payment. And in item 2, we can see that a report was attached, report regarding the overall assistance provided to the SDS, I assume for the period between May and November, and the amount is approximately 3.050.000 German marks. So what I heard as rumours is actually confirmed in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now I'll turn to -- Mr. Deronjic, if I could have -- actually, let me have Prosecutor's Exhibit 35 put back on the monitor, if I could. And Mr. Deronjic, while Prosecutor's Exhibit 35 is coming up on the monitor: In very late March or early April, did the Serbs in Eastern Bosnia start to seize power in municipalities that were adjacent to the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. If my memory serves me right, I think they began around the 1st of April. They started with Bijeljina, I think. Q.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Bijeljina, Your Honours, is the upper right-hand corner municipality in Prosecutor's Exhibit 35.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did they -- did those seizures of power continue, Mr. Deronjic, in municipalities that were near you following Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. After Bijeljina, and I think that the events in Bijeljina are very well known, the conflict extended to Zvornik. Similar units took part in this. I am referring first and foremost to Arkan's units, I mean Zeljko Raznatovic, Arkan's units, including a number of volunteer units that took part in the takeover of power by Serbs. However, the situation was somewhat more complicated there, and I can explain if you want me to. These conflicts then went on in the region of Podrinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And which municipalities, Mr. Deronjic? And I'm particularly interested in the municipalities where the seizure of power occurred before it occurred in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall try to enumerate the municipalities I'm aware of: Bijeljina, Zvornik, Srebrenica, Visegrad. These are Podrinje municipalities. As far as I know from the media, the conflicts also concerned Banja Luka and a number of other municipalities which I cannot remember at this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, the Visegrad municipality is found at the bottom right-hand side of the map that is before you, and the Srebrenica municipality is directly above it. So in a line, the municipalities that have been identified by Mr. Deronjic start at the top: Bijeljina, come down to Zvornik, pass by Bratunac, and then you come on the right-hand side to Srebrenica and to Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, were you able to discern a pattern, a rough pattern, in respect of the forces that were used in the takeover and seizure of power in these particular municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. There was a pattern of behaviour, of conduct of the participants in those events, which is almost identical for all these municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- we suggest that it should be made clear, following his answer a few minutes ago, when he said he would try to enumerate the municipalities he was aware of, and he referred to Bijeljina, Zvornik, Srebrenica, and Visegrad as the Podrinje municipalities. And then he said: "As far as I know from the media, the conflicts also concerned Banja Luka and a number of other municipalities." There seems to be at least a distinct possibility, if not a probability, that what Mr. Deronjic knows in relation to any municipalities outside his own municipality of Bratunac is simply gleaned from the media. That should be clarified first, because if that is the source of his information, then it's inappropriate that this line of questioning should continue with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll be glad to clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, were you in contact with people from the Bijeljina municipality, from the Zvornik municipality, from the Srebrenica municipality, and from the Visegrad municipality, and did they relate to you the way in which power was taken over, the forces that were used in the takeover of power in those particular municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, that's an outrageously leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but it follows the answer already given in line -- page 11, line 17, so I would not deny Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Line 17, Your Honour. Line 17 is part of my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 11.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 11, line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He enumerated the municipalities. He seems to have a different base of knowledge than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, seems to have. Your Honour, we haven't established that yet. That was precisely the purpose of my intervention. And although that might be the position, that's what's important to establish, and it is important, we suggest, to establish these things without complicated, composite leading questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Deronjic, you testified that you were aware of Bijeljina, Zvornik, Srebrenica, Visegrad, when answering a question on the takeover of the power. Could you tell us how you became aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With respect to certain municipalities, I was able to learn directly what happened, for instance, the municipality of Srebrenica, I was personally present in the area when the volunteers arrived. Likewise for the Bratunac municipality, I directly participated in it. As for the municipality of Zvornik, I never went there when these events were taking place. However, some of the people did, members of the crisis staff, for instance, and they conveyed to me the information as to what was going on in Zvornik. I even reached a decision once to ban people from going to Zvornik for that reason. I have never been to Bijeljina personally. I know about these events in Bijeljina indirectly, and I know about it from a later period ,because I knew a number of people who had a significant role in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you said that some people of the crisis staff went there, do you mean the Bratunac Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I was referring to the Crisis Staff of the Serbian people in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, based on those contacts and the information you received, were you able to discern a pattern in respect of the forces that were used in the takeover of those municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I was about to tell you about that. It was a complex process indeed, and quite dramatic at the moment. Perhaps I was not able during those first days to assess the situation and to analyse it properly. However, during the war and through the contacts with people, I discussed the events of April 1992 quite often, and I have a clear picture as to what was going on in the area of Podrinje at the time. When I say, "a clear picture," I don't think I -- I'm not trying to say that I have an entire picture of the events, but I do have certain knowledge. The arrival of those units which are referred to as volunteers, including Arkan's units, in an area where there is no conflict, at least not an open conflict, it is obvious that they arrive with a certain objective on their mind. During those first days, a large number of people, a large number of Muslims, were killed. As for the participation of the JNA during that period, they did not try to prevent these conflicts. I was personally able to see the participation of the JNA in Bratunac, and I also had information that in Zvornik, for instance, the JNA had sided with the Serbs. Let me also say that the commander who arrived in Bratunac, which is what I learned subsequently, Mr. Reljic, had a role in the events in Bijeljina as well. I'm not sure as to what exactly he had done there, but I know that the JNA units had sided with the Serbs. As for the arrival of the volunteers, the aim was to provoke the conflict. Their acts were intended to intimidate the population, to create an atmosphere of terror, and, to a certain extent, this behaviour concerned also Serbs, or rather, non-loyal Serbs, so to speak, which all resulted in the change of the ethnic structure of the area. A large number of Muslims eventually left. And once again, a large number of people were killed during that period. So this would have been the pattern that I was able to observe and that I already discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I'd like to now focus your attention on the arrival of volunteers in your municipality, and I'd like to take you back to the 14th or 15th of April, 1992. Can you tell the Trial Chamber about the facts and circumstances relating to the arrival of volunteers in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. On the 17th of April, volunteers arrived in the municipality of Bratunac. They came in the morning hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we get to the actual arrival, I'd like to take you back a few days earlier, to a situation when you actually travelled to a particular location and observed volunteers for the first time. Can you tell the Trial Chamber the circumstances of those events.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My apologies. I understood your question to refer to Bratunac exclusively. Your Honours, I saw the volunteers for the first time sometime around the 14th of April, 1992, in Bajina Basta. Bajina Basta is an adjacent municipality to the municipality of Srebrenica, and partly to the municipality of Bratunac as well. It was upon the invitation of Mr. Goran Zekic, whom we have already mentioned, I went with a friend of mine to Bajina Basta early that morning, because I had been asked to come to the Territorial Defence of the Bajina Basta municipality. I found the building easily, because Bajina Basta is a rather small town. I entered the yard of that building and was then taken to the office where Mr. Zekic was. He was there together with the chief of staff of the Bajina Basta Territorial Defence, Mr. Bijelic [phoen], and a gentleman by the name of Miodrag Jokic, who was the vice-president of the Srebrenica chapter of SDS. I saw a large number of volunteers in the yard of that building, people in uniform, who appeared to be preparing themselves for some military activity. I asked Mr. Zekic what this was all about and he told me that they were members of a unit that had arrived in Srebrenica with a certain mission to carry out in Srebrenica, and they were completing their arrival in Skelani. These volunteers were already armed and in uniform in the yard of the Territorial Defence building, and they were waiting to head off to Skelani, which is a town in the municipality of Srebrenica. Shortly after that, this particular unit started to march through the centre of Bajina Basta in the direction of Skelani, which is situated some two kilometres away from Bajina Basta, right across the Drina River. I was at the back of this column of volunteers, because Zekic had asked me whether I wanted to join them so that we could continue with the meeting in Skelani. I crossed the bridge, still in this column, which was moving freely through Bajina Basta. Even the police helped regulate the traffic in the town at that moment. We arrived. We crossed the bridge and we went to the other side. They were armed, but nobody caused any problems. The police allowed them to cross over to Skelani. I stayed there for a while. Goran Zekic went to the police building and the newly established town hall. I don't know what they had in terms of offices. They came Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. back in about ten minutes. I was still on the parking lot of this building. I was wearing civilian clothes. I had a civilian vehicle. And he asked -- he told me that they were going to Srebrenica and he asked me whether I wanted to join them. I said I was not ready. I wanted to go back to Bratunac. And once again, I asked him what this was all about, and he said that we would see each other shortly in the upcoming days and that he would tell me about them, but briefly, he just told me that they were just members of a unit that had arrived in Srebrenica. I returned to Bratunac, and Mr. Zekic went with that unit in the direction of Srebrenica. These were my first experiences and my first encounter with the volunteers. And what I was able to see that day, based on that, I formed some conclusions that that pattern that I talked about was spreading in the neighbouring municipalities and that this was not an accident, either in Bijeljina or Zvornik. These were not just local incidents, but all of that had a broader significance. When I came back to Bratunac, I expected that Bratunac would soon also be caught up in the same problems and that some unit would also appear there. On the 17th of April, a unit did happen to come --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, we'll get to there in just a minute. But let me ask you, Mr. Deronjic: When you were in Bajina Basta and you were there with Mr. Zekic and Miodrag Jokic, did Mr. Zekic say who was responsible for bringing the volunteers to Bajina Basta?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did, but what he said does not have to be true. I even think that it wasn't true. When I asked him who brought those volunteers, he said it was Miodrag Jokic who did that. He had some connections in Serbia, and he had brought these people. I think that that is not true. And Goran Zekic sometimes likes to make some jokes in that way. He even was laughing when he said that. I think that there were contacts between him and somebody who sent that unit. It's possible that what he said was also true, but I did not check on that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Deronjic, you described -- you said, and I made a note of it, even the police helped regulate traffic in the movement of the paramilitaries through Serbia into Bosnia. Can you, just very quickly, describe what it was that the police did to assist the volunteers in their movements.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would just like to ask: I once had in the translation that the army helped, and the second time it was that the police helped. I apologise. I talked about solely the assistance of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. Again, I'm asking you only in respect of the police in Serbia. What actions did they take to assist the movements of the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The police regulated traffic. There was a special traffic regime at the time which was evident. When we left the TO building, headquarters, which is in the centre of town, all the streets that we went through were blocked for traffic. There was a police car at the head of the column. I'm not sure whether there was also one at the rear of the column. You could clearly see the weapons in the hands of those people in the vehicles. Most of them also had their weapons sticking out through the windows. The traffic regime was such that I could see that the traffic lights were all coordinated in the same way. There was just the blinking yellow light, indicating that the passage was free, with some caution. There was a number of people who were observing what was happening from the sidewalk, and this was quite incredible in those circumstances. It was the first time I had seen anything like it, and it looked quite unusual. I thought that if this was going to be done, it should be done in some kind of secret manner. But the way it was happening, it was actually happening in broad daylight, and the police was informed about the movements of those people. There's also the border police on the bridge, and I did not notice that they were stopping or checking anyone, on either side of the bridge. So that's what I meant when I said that the police took part in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Approximately how many volunteers went across into Bosnia when you were present?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a clear idea. I think that there were perhaps some ten vehicles. And if you take into account that there were perhaps three or four people in each vehicle, then we're talking perhaps about 30 or 40 people who crossed into Skelani at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did these volunteers wear any identifying insignia or patches on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't notice any at the time. Perhaps I just wasn't paying attention, but I didn't notice any insignia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, I want to go -- that was to another day, and another topic, and we'll return to the issue of the volunteers shortly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON

But it was reported on the 16th while the previous decision is dated the 16th, if I remember well. I must say that due to an absence of a consistent way of communicating with the republican leadership, we adapted our activities to what we could learn from the media, and I'm stating that the TO of Republika Srpska was formed on the 15th of April, 1992. And I think that there were reports about this on the 15th of April. And we decided, and this is mentioned here, based on the decision of the Presidency of the Republic of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina on general mobilisation. So we adopted our decision in Bratunac based on that decision. This minor problem about the dates I think can be clarified in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On the original B/C/S version there's a signature at the bottom. Whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my signature, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, let me return briefly to -- actually, let me stay with this document. What did you do after you issued this particular order? Were people mobilised?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not mobilised, in the classic sense, that the army units were being formed. No. This was more a declaration in adherence to the decision of the republican organ. At that time, Muslims were present in the governing bodies in Bratunac. We were sharing power with them at the time. And immediately prior to these events, we held a Joint Assembly session. It was impossible to organise people, to mobilise them, and place them in barracks, military barracks, because there were no such facilities available. It was more a proclamation stating that if the need arose, people were duty-bound to report for mobilisation.
