utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, now I'd like to turn your attention to the 17th of April, 1992, in the morning, and I would like you to tell the Judges what happened that particular morning.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly, Mr. Harmon and Your Honours: That morning, armed people appeared at the Fontana Hotel. As far as I could tell at that time, it was a group consisting of about 30 people. I was at home, and a message reached me to come to the Fontana Hotel as soon as possible, to attend a meeting, because soldiers had arrived. So I went there, and as I was getting into the hotel, I noticed that Goran Zekic was present at the meeting, as well as Mr. Miodrag Jokic, whom I mentioned earlier on, who was the vice-president of the Srebrenica SDS, and Velibor Sorak, a man from Srebrenica as well, who was also present at the meeting. Apart from them, I remember seeing three men in uniform present there as well. On the opposite side of the table, there were representatives of the Muslims from Srebrenica. As far as I can recall, Ljubisav Simic, the then-president of the Serbian Municipal Assembly, was also present. At that moment, he was actually leaving the meeting. When I arrived, I noticed that the hotel had been blocked by these people in uniform, and I realised that those were the same -- or rather, the similar individuals as the ones that I had seen in Bajina Basta a few days earlier. So I entered the hotel. I inquired as to what the meeting was about, and Mr. Zekic told me that the meeting was with the representatives of the Srebrenica Muslims. He told me who they were. One of the volunteers, who obviously was there on behalf of the commander of the unit, said that they had given an ultimatum of the Bratunac Muslim representatives that they should abandon power, that this concerned the police station and that the deadline was 12.00 on that day, that is, that they had to leave all institutions by that time. They wanted me and Ljubisav Simic to give them a list of extremists, as they called them. Mr. Simic got very angry. He said he wished to take no part in that. He left the meeting. He said he did not have any list. I believe I already quoted his words in my interview. I stayed at the meeting briefly and was informed that the Muslim leadership wanted to see me, that they were at the public security station in Bratunac and they wanted to see me there. It was one of the waiters who brought me the message that had arrived by telephone. So I went to the police station, the public security station in Bratunac, where I found the president of the municipality, Mr. Dubicic, the president of the Bratunac municipal board of the SDA, Mr. Dzevad Gusic; the chief of police, whose last name was Hodzic. I cannot remember his first name; and two other individuals, secondary school teacher who was a member of the municipal SDA, Numo Pleho was his name. They wanted to know who the people at the Fontana Hotel were, and I told them that I did not know who they were, that that was the first time that I'd seen them. They asked if I could guarantee their security. I said that I couldn't because I didn't know who those people were. This is just the gist of our conversation. They wanted to know if I could organise their departure from Bratunac. They wanted to know if they could have a vehicle, because they wanted to go to Konjevic, which is a Muslim village in the direction of Tuzla, because apparently there were problems there, and they wanted to see what they can do to calm down the situation. I said that there should be no problems about that, that they should take the police car, and I mentioned potential problems in the village of Kravica, which is a predominantly Serb village. Actually, correction. They mentioned this village, and I said that there shouldn't be any problems there because I had given them my consent to go there. It was my assumption that they wanted to leave Bratunac, which turned out to be true. So they took this vehicle and left in the direction of Tuzla. From what I learnt subsequently, they left the municipality on that day. The police station remained rather empty. I noticed the fact that the majority of Muslim police officers had left the station. I assumed that they had been informed by their chief. A few individuals remained, including two or three Serb officers who were sitting on the stairs of the building. By that time, it was already noon, I think, and the unit which was at the Fontana Hotel had in the meantime started walking toward the police station. They got to the entrance to the police station. I stopped them there. I told them that there was no use -- that they should not use weapons, that the leadership of the police station had left, and that the station was, practically speaking, empty. They entered the premises. They stayed there for half an hour. Then they took the vehicles and left with Goran Zekic in the direction of Srebrenica. They drove in a column. So I had no time to go back to the Fontana Hotel. They had already left for Srebrenica. And this is how that day ended. And this is just a brief description of what I think is the most important -- the most important events of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, the men who were inside the Hotel Fontana and the men who were outside of the Fontana, did you believe that those men were the people who had been volunteers and who had accompanied Mr. Zekic and Mr. Jokic to Skelani?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a conclusion that I was able to reach, yes, but I did not recognise any of the people attending the Fontana meeting. I had not seen them in Bajina Basta. But they did resemble those people, as far as their uniforms and weapons are concerned. I'm not 100 per cent sure that they were the same individuals, but I think that some of them were the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You said weapons. Were they all armed, and can you describe what type of arms they were carrying?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all armed, and so far as I could observe, they all carried automatic infantry weapons, automatic rifles, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, when the -- when you went over and had a conversation with the Bosnian Muslim leaders from the Bratunac municipality, and they asked you who are those people, you said you didn't know. Why did you say you didn't know?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really didn't know who they were. I had never seen any of them before. I could not even recognise them as individuals who had been in Bajina Basta before that. Subsequently, I learned that one of them was one of the leaders of the group that had been in Bajina Basta the previous day. But again, I had never seen them in my life prior to that. I had never had any contact with them. Goran Zekic didn't have enough time to tell me who they were, because I had to go to the police station. The only thing that I could perhaps assume was that they were the volunteers who had come from Serbia, with the mission to expel Muslims from the government in Bratunac. But I said that I didn't know who they were because I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when, Mr. Deronjic, was it that the Bosnian Serbs took over power in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right after this event, all institutions in Bratunac were, practically speaking, dissolved, because most of the employees had been Muslims. I'm referring to the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, the police, and other judiciary and administrative, both state and republican organs. Only Serbs remained. And we seized power, de facto speaking, sometime in late April 1992. At that time, we had already established the crisis staff of the Bratunac municipality, the municipal crisis staff, which means that we functioned -- we continued to function for a while as the crisis staff of the Serbian people, which had been established in October the previous year. And later that month, we established the Bratunac Municipal Crisis Staff, because conditions had been met in the meantime. That is, the relevant bodies had been established, the police and so on and so forth. And by virtue of their functions, the chiefs of such organs became members of the municipal crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, these volunteers that had assisted in the takeover of power in Bratunac on the 17th of April, did they return to Bratunac and did they remain in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not remain in Bratunac. They went to Srebrenica, where they stayed, and continued with their activities. A conflict was soon to break out between Serbs and Muslims in Srebrenica. By that time, these conflicts were already opened, and they involved murders as well. They would come to Bratunac by night in police vehicles --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you this question, Mr. Deronjic: What can you tell the Judges what these volunteers did in Bratunac after the takeover of power on the 17th of April? How did they behave themselves?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was about to tell you how it happened. They came to Bratunac mostly by night. They created panic. They opened fire in the streets. They drove their vehicles very fast, with sirens. They entered various streets in the town by night and started plundering property. They seized private property from individual Muslims. I'm referring to their cars mostly, because people started complaining about that fact. They killed -- I'm not sure about the date, but they killed during that period of time several Muslim individuals in Bratunac. One family was murdered. Two or three brothers, I think they were, were killed during that period. And another two individuals in Zljevice, a suburb, the incident we learned about later on. So they were creating panic around the town. They arrested people, robbed them of their property, of their personal belongings, and, yes, those were the most drastic examples of their activity during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And were Bosnian Serbs who lived in Bratunac also terrorised by these people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were many examples of that. I did not speak about it at length, but there were many cases of harassment of Serbs, including arrests, also of the members of the crisis staff during that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what happened to these particular -- this particular group of volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Three days after the arrival in Bratunac, on the 20th of April, 1992, to be precise, the Muslims, that is, their armed forces - and this is what I know from reports. I do not have any direct knowledge of that - under the command of Naser Oric, laid an ambush in Potocari, and most of the volunteers were killed in this ambush. Potocari is five kilometres away from the centre of Bratunac, so territorially speaking, it's part of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, had you seen these particular volunteers in their cars with stolen goods, and could you describe -- if yes, could you describe to the Court what you saw.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an opportunity of seeing them personally. These are very small towns, after all. And I also had information from the people in my close surroundings that they were engaged in plunder of some technical goods in Srebrenica. At that time, this would have been more difficult to carry out in Bratunac, but Srebrenica was plundered and the goods were taken then to Bratunac and across the bridge linking the area with Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after the first group of volunteers was killed by the forces of Naser Oric, what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two things happened, two things which would be of some significance for the future development of events. A JNA unit arrived in the area. I had never seen this unit before, nor did I have any knowledge in that period as to the identity of that unit. But it was an armoured unit, consisting of perhaps 20 troops and 5 to 6 armoured vehicles. Captain Suljic was their leader. I think they arrived in Bratunac on the 21st or 22nd. I'm not a hundred per cent sure of those dates, but I know that it was immediately after the murder of the volunteers in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Reljic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we get to the arrival of the JNA, just let me ask you: In respect of the volunteers who had been killed, what happened to those volunteers, the bodies of those volunteers? And did another group of volunteers arrive?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just wanted to link the two events. We made an effort to obtain the bodies and to recover them to the territory of the Bratunac municipality so that we could hand them over to their families. Attempts were made to negotiate with the people from Potocari. The president, Mr. Simic, played an important role in this, together with a number of members of the police, including a Muslim man who assisted us a lot in this. Mr. Reljic had arrived in the meantime, and I think he joined in the negotiations with the other side, with the purpose of obtaining the bodies. During that period -- again, I'm not sure about the date, but it could have been either the 23rd or the 24th -- a group of -- a large group of volunteers arrived in Serbia. It was my estimate that it consisted of about a hundred armed men. And they sent an invitation for me to come to Ljubovija to negotiate. And I went to Ljubovija and I can testify about that if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, in brief, were the bodies of the slain volunteers returned to their people?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Several bodies - I don't remember the exact number. I don't think we actually managed to find them all - were obtained. They were handed over by Naser during those negotiations and they were brought to Bratunac. Families were informed of that through the media, I guess. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic -- [Previous translation continues]... Additional details that the Defence or the Court wants to ask you some questions about that element of your testimony they can. But let me then ask you,

utterances.speaker: MR. DERONJIC
utterances.text: Did another group of volunteers arrive in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have already mentioned this very large group of volunteers who had arrived in Ljubovija. I went there. I wanted to prevent their entering the area. Together with me was Mr. Milutin Milosevic, the chief from Bratunac. We didn't want them to get into Bratunac, and we informed them of that. However, part of that large group entered the town of Bratunac on their own initiative, later on, and they stayed until mid-May. They insisted that they should all get in Bratunac, under the pretext of wanting to obtain those bodies. But we knew that that was not their real mission. We just talked to two or three of their representatives. But, however, in the course of the following days, this smaller group of volunteers managed to get into town, where they stayed until mid-May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why didn't you want the volunteers in Bratunac after the 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible for me at that time to see clearly for myself what it is that they were engaged in and to what extent we could have any influence over them. When we went to see them, me -- I and Mr. Reljic, our attitude was that we should not let them in, because a hundred armed people without any control constituted a danger, that is, a danger for us, because we couldn't have any control over the events, and that is the reason why we didn't want them in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How many volunteers in the smaller group would you estimate arrived in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Correction of the interpreter. Not Mr. Reljic, but Mr. Zekic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think about 20. Those were not permanent groups, you see, and their number varied, which meant that they did not have very strict control and command. Some of the troops would leave and when -- and go to another area. But I know that there were about 20 of them at all times.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did these -- this new group of volunteers that had arrived in Bratunac, did they -- how did they conduct themselves in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I must say that probably because of the presence of the military, they were not so aggressive as the first group. However, harassment of the Muslims, including the plunder, continued. But we tried to manage as best as we could with the assistance of the police. However, there were no murders during that period when this second group arrived; at least, I don't remember any.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of people were these people who were in the volunteers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will be direct. There were mostly criminals. And in the later period, I had the opportunity to check some things. The majority of those people were criminals, even a large number of them were released from prison with the intention that they should take part in these volunteer units. Later I got to know some of them, and I believe that they were mostly criminals, which was evident from their behaviour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was the leader of this volunteer -- small volunteer group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The volunteer group was headed by a person nicknamed Peki. This is how we knew him in the beginning. Later I found out that his name was Predrag Cubrilo and that he was from a village in Vojvodina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you identify by name other members of the volunteer group?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult to do it by name, but I knew their nicknames. I knew some of their -- I knew some of them by nicknames. I remembered the name of one of them, if that was his real name. I recall the names of some other people. There was Zoran Kosijer. I remember that name. Then there was a girl, Dragica Mastikosa. She was killed later. Most had nicknames such Makedonac, Niski, Tihi, nicknames like that. Rambo. These are some of the nicknames that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, given the concerns that you and others in the Bratunac municipality had in respect of these paramilitaries, did the crisis staff take any action vis-a-vis these volunteer groups? And you can answer that yes or no, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did take some steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have the next two exhibits given an identification -- given an exhibit number. The first will be the one that is dated -- document dated May 1st, 1992 in the upper left-hand corner of the first page.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit number P56, and the following document, Exhibit P57.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Your Honours, over the recess I had copies of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. these made and distributed, I hope, to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's highly appreciated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, while these are being distributed, if you could just cast on eye on Exhibits P56 and P57, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with these crisis staff decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me, Mr. Deronjic, direct your attention, first of all, to P56. On the B/C/S version, at the bottom of that document, there appears to be a signature. Can you identify that signature?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the signature of the crisis staff's secretary. Sometimes we would agree that when a decision was typed out, and if I was not present, then the secretary would sign it. Zoran Tesic was the crisis staff's secretary and this is his signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: On P57 also whose signature appears on the bottom of that exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, starting with P56, can you just enlighten us as to that particular exhibit. What is it, and why was it promulgated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I will be as brief as possible. The decisions banning the activities of all paramilitary formations in the territory of Bratunac municipality was adopted on May 1st. The reason for this was the conduct of the volunteers and the constant clashes between the police, which was already formed as the Serbian police in Bratunac, and the chief of the municipality -- actually, the chief of the station, Mr. Milosevic, who conveyed this information to us and asked us to adopt a decision allowing him to sanction the conduct of these volunteers. We adopted such a decision, and as far as I know, I have that also, that decision, amongst my documents, as well as some documents on the expulsion and arrest of the most extremist of the volunteers from the group. That's the first document. The second document is also about what I'm just explaining. It's a decision allowing the police legally to disarm those illegal groups which appeared. And I can tell you that in that period, in other areas of the municipality, it was noticed that some unknown people were crossing over the Drina with weapons. So these decisions referred to all of these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you have mentioned, and I have stopped you from proceeding at this point, on the arrival of a JNA unit into Bratunac. Can you first of all tell us approximately when did a unit of the JNA arrive in the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you the precise date, but I believe that this was immediately following the killing of the volunteers in Potocari. I think that that date was the 20th -- the 21st, the 22nd, or the 23rd of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What kind of a unit was it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a smaller unit of the JNA. It was an armoured unit with five or six armoured vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the number of men in that unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It comprised mostly the crews of the armoured vehicles and a number of the police. They were wearing military police uniforms. The total was about 20 people, according to my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say an armoured unit, what type of armoured vehicles were they?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there were four personnel carriers. These are armoured personnel carriers. And a tank. I know that there was a tank. Then there was a smaller armoured vehicle, which I think is called a combat armoured vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was the commander of this particular unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Reljic. I cannot remember the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was his rank?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you know where this particular military unit came from?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They came from Sekovici, from a unit which was located in the Sekovici municipality. It is the headquarters of an armoured, mechanised brigade, whose commander was a Mr. Tacic. I don't remember his first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, upon the arrival of Captain Reljic in the JNA unit, what actions did they take in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They first introduced military rule. Then they adopted a plan on the disarming of Muslims, or extremists, this is what they called it, on the territory of the Bratunac municipality. They were referring to Muslim settlements. The plan was adopted at a meeting without the crisis staff. It was held at a -- one company in Bratunac, at their building. And then at a meeting of the crisis staff, they informed us about the plan, which we verified, even though some disarming activities had already started without the knowledge of the crisis staff. These were the first actions undertaken by Mr. Reljic in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, when you say in your testimony they first introduced military rule, how did they do that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Reljic printed some posters, and he put them up all over Bratunac, informing the people. I had the opportunity to read this poster. Informing people that military rule was introduced, and he proclaimed himself the commander of town. This is how he signed it: Captain Reljic, so-and-so, and that he was responsible for the situation in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I take it, Mr. Deronjic, that after -- on the 17th, when the leadership, the Bosnian Muslim leadership of Bratunac, left, many, many, many Muslims in the settlements, the Muslim settlements, indeed remained in the Bratunac municipality. Is that a fair assertion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is absolutely true. They were mostly leaving the territory of the Bratunac municipality from town. This was before the conflict started in Bijeljina, in Zvornik. While in the villages of Bratunac, they still remained. They didn't leave the villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, what was the characterisation by Captain Reljic and the purpose of this disarming campaign?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the disarming plan and the conduct of the army in Bratunac was something that he discussed at a meeting without the presence of the crisis staff, with people who were not members of the crisis staff. After he took over control, from that point on he was issuing commands to the TO for the mobilisation of soldiers, so that Muslim villages would be disarmed. Already in late April, some disarming activities were carried out in Muslim villages. At a subsequent meeting of the crisis staff, he tabled this decision. We discussed it. There was no particular need for it to be explained to us, because we saw what the result was of previous actions. It was to collect weapons in Muslim villages and to warehouse them at a depot of the police station in Bratunac. That was the purpose of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Deronjic, did you participate in one of the actions to disarm a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I joined a TO unit which was leaving that day, and I joined them in the capacity of soldier, because I was mobilised in the action to disarm the village of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the name of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name of the village? The interpreter didn't hear the name of it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Podcaus.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe to the Judges the manner in which the disarming of the village that you saw occurred. What was the modus operandi?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early in the morning, before dawn, the TO units of Bratunac received orders -- at that point they were comprising exclusively Serbs. They received an order to occupy a village, to surround it, and not to come too close to it but at a distance from it, upon the order of Commander Reljic, all the soldiers were supposed to fire one bullet into the air in order to let the Muslims in that village know that they were surrounded. That was the only task that we had as soldiers. After that, police would enter, the police and the army, with armoured vehicles, would enter the village, and then via loudspeaker they would call on the people to surrender their illegal and even legal weapons. If they had a licence for hunting weapons, they were supposed to bring them along. That was how the action proceeded. The villagers did respond. I wasn't present in the village to see how many people actually came out, but people did come out and hand over their weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did the JNA make any assurances to the people who had surrendered their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. I think that Mr. Reljic said that he did issue some receipts or certificates. I wasn't present in the village, but I think that he did give some kind of written receipt for the arms that were confiscated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just intervene. I don't know whether I understood your earlier answer correct. You said in the village when people were ordered to hand over their weapons, whether legal or illegal, would that be for all the villages or just for a certain part of the villages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This applied to all the villages. But Your Honour, I would like to underscore that we are talking about villages now that have a completely Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because I see it's about the -- your answer starts to be about villages, where my question was, as I see in the transcript, about villagers. But now you continued. You said in these villages there would live exclusively Muslim population, do I understand that correctly, not one Serb, not one Croat, not one other nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. Perhaps there was the odd villager like that, but I don't know. Not in that village, though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I was going to ask you: What were the Muslim villages that were disarmed? Can you identify those Muslim villages for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that action. Then I remember Glogova, which was also disarmed in that period, up until May. I remember a village called Lolici or Hrnjici in Konjevic Polje. I'm not sure. I wasn't there. These are the villages that I remember for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there a settlement known as Voljevica? I may have slaughtered the pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that settlement, but I cannot remember exactly whether Voljevica was amongst them. At this moment, I don't remember. If I remember later, I will tell you, but I'm not sure right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, now I'm going to -- Mr. Deronjic, how long did this disarming campaign last? When did it end?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It ended in early May. I don't know the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn your attention now to the village of Glogova and the attack on that village that took place on the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have the assistance of the usher to put the following exhibit on the stand. This, Your Honours, is an exhibit. It's four pages. If we could put it on the ELMO, then I can direct your attention to certain portions of it. If that could be given an exhibit number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, while the usher is putting this map on the ELMO, have you had a chance to familiarise yourself with the map?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, Mr. Harmon, could I ask you one question? It says it's a 1:100.000 scale. Can the Chamber be sure that it's not enlarged or reduced in size? Because that immediately affects the scale.
