utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, we're going to focus for a few minutes on the village of Glogova, and what I'd like you to do is -- there should be a pointer, Mr. Deronjic. The usher is handing you a pointer, and you'll see on the ELMO, the machine to your left, there is a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Usher, perhaps you can show him how the pointer works on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What I'd like you to do, Mr. Deronjic, is you can get out of your chair, approach the map on the ELMO, and I'm going to ask you some questions about the village of Glogova. Mr. Deronjic, can you first of all tell the Judges: What was the strategic importance of the village of Glogova? And you can use that pointer to illustrate your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Glogova is on the road between Bratunac and Kravica. Kravica, let me just mention it to the Trial Chamber, is a region comprising a number of Serbian villages, and it's right behind Glogova, in the direction towards Konjevic Polje. There is a crossroads there. One of the roads leads to Pale, another -- for Sarajevo, and the other leads to Zvornik from those crossroads. Glogova is located halfway -- about seven kilometres away from Bratunac, so it is halfway to Kravica. And it's the only Serb region in the municipality of Bratunac which is respectable. It encompasses a large territory and has a large number of Serb inhabitants. It is exactly on the road at an elevation - I'm talking about the village of Glogova now - it's a dominant village in that region. It is on the -- on both sides of this key road towards the rest of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's where the village of Glogova is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, based on the -- you can have a seat again, Mr. Deronjic. Thank you for that explanation. Mr. Deronjic, I'm just looking at the transcript of your testimony. It says as follows: "Glogova is located halfway, about seven kilometres away from Bratunac, so it is halfway to Kravica. And it's the only Serb region in the municipality of Bratunac which is respectable." I take it you're referring to Kravica being the only Serb region in the municipality of Bratunac which is respectable; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant to say -- I was thinking of Kravica, but I know that there are some kind of -- that this is maybe not quite clear. I was thinking of Kravica, but it came out a little bit ambivalent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. So to summarise, Mr. Deronjic: Between Bratunac and the Serb settlement of Kravica, Glogova, a predominantly Muslim village, was in between; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, based on your conclusion that Glogova had a strategic importance, did you come to a decision in your own mind as to what needed to be done in respect of the village of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honours, I came to a decision that the village of Glogova, that is, that the population of the village of Glogova should be forcibly resettled from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, we're going to go into some details in respect of that particular attack, but let me focus your attention to a meeting that took place between you and Mr. Zekic, Goran Zekic, on the 4th or the 5th of May, in the Hotel Fontana. Do you recall that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that meeting. I remember the details of my conversation with Mr. Zekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges how that meeting came about and what occurred at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was an accidental encounter of myself with Mr. Zekic. Actually, it was the first opportunity that we had to be alone after the events in Bratunac and Skelani involving the volunteers. I wanted to know, and I wanted to hear from Goran Zekic, what it was that he knew about the arrival of volunteers in Bratunac, about their intentions and their plans, about their commander, and other things that were of interest to me. Because of the events in Srebrenica, I had not seen Goran Zekic before that. I may have seen him in passing, but I did not have opportunity to be with him alone. It was impossible for me to travel in the area, because Potocari were under the Muslim control. So during that encounter, I asked him the following: What was the role of the volunteers? What was the role of the military in Bratunac and Srebrenica? And what was actually happening in all these municipalities in Podrinje, where the conflicts at the time were already open? I wanted to know if he knew more about these events and what it was that he could tell me about it. He provided me with certain information, basically telling me that it would be wise for me to stay away from the military, not to have any influence over the military. He was aware of my conflict with the military and the volunteers, and his advice basically was for me to stay away from them. I wanted to know under whose orders they were acting, and he said one sentence, which I remembered to this date, that this was all pursuant to an agreement and that the arrival of the military in Bratunac had been based on an agreement between the leadership of Serbia and the leadership of Republika Srpska. So this would be the gist of my conversation with Mr. Zekic at Fontana on the 4th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was this plan or agreement that was described by Mr. Zekic something that Mr. Zekic could conceive on his own?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. This would have been impossible. It would have been impossible for him to have any control whatsoever over the forces in Serbia and the Territorial Defence and the police, who provided assistance to the arrival of these volunteers. He did not have any jurisdiction whatsoever in that area. This must have been -- this had to be agreed upon on a much higher level. Likewise, the arrival of the military and their activities, I don't think that that had anything to do with the agreement of Zekic with these individuals but that this was agreed upon at the military top and those activities could not have been undertaken pursuant to Zekic's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when Mr. Zekic said that an agreement between the leadership of Serbia and the leadership of Republika Srpska, did you come to any conclusions in respect of who he meant?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have to say that his opinion was only a confirmation of what I thought. Such broad action, according to a certain set pattern, this could not be an isolated phenomenon in the area. This must have been -- had to be coordinated at a very high level. When he said this to me, I know that he was referring to the highest organs of Republika Srpska, which had already been established and was already functioning as a real state, and the leadership of Serbia. So I presume that he referred to the highest-positioned leaders in Serbia at that moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who, Mr. Deronjic, were the highest-positioned leaders in the Republika Srpska - can I finish my question, please - on the time you had this conversation with Mr. Zekic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please, before answering this question, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, Mr. Harmon has already adduced some evidence about who the highest-positioned leaders in Republika Srpska were, and there is plenty of evidence about that. It's clear what he's trying to do here. He's trying to get this witness to make the links that Mr. Harmon wants for his case. But the way he put it when he said in his question: When Mr. Zekic said that an agreement between the leadership of Serbia and the leadership of Republika Srpska, did you come to any conclusions in respect of who he meant? Now, I refrained from objecting there, but really the question ought consistently with the suggestions we made yesterday to be phrased in terms of: Did you know who he meant? Rather than conclusions. Because that strays once again into the area of opinion. If this witness did not know who Mr. Zekic meant specifically, then he should not be pushed into saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, your testimony was that you presumed that Mr. Zekic was referring to the highest-positioned leaders in Serbia at that moment, and you also testified that you knew that he was referring to the highest organs of the Republika Srpska, which had already been established. So you said you presumed the highest level in Serbia and that you knew that he was referring to the highest levels of Republika Srpska. Could you tell us what made you know and what in his wordings made you presume. So I'd like to know, on the basis of what he said to you, what caused you or for whatever other reason you would know he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect, we're not absolutely sure. We'll stand corrected if it appears on the transcript, but at the moment we're not absolutely sure that he used the word "knew." He certainly said he presumed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but a few lines prior to that. His presumption was in relation to the Republic of Serbia, according to the transcript, and if you look six, seven, eight lines before, he said, "I knew that he was referring to the highest authorities of --" but let me just check.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. I only wanted to check. I'm not asserting that that's wrong, Your Honour. Just it's an important area. We just want to be sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can return -- I'll read it for you and I'll give you the lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can return -- I'll read it to you and I'll give you the lines. Let's just have a look. Page 55, line 5, starting at line 4, he says, about the coordination: "When he said this to me, I know that he was referring to the highest organs of the Republika Srpska, which had already been established." And then two lines later, he says: "So I presume that he referred to the highest-positioned leaders in Serbia at that moment." So as I just made a distinction between --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. We're stuck at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Page 55.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your presumption, you find it in line 7. What he knew was in line 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I just don't know what's happening here, because we're looking specifically at something which is numbered page 55 and we're getting something completely different. I don't know what the mechanical explanation of that is. We're just getting something totally different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You're not looking in another transcript or something like that? No. No. I can -- no. It's always a matter of analysing the problems. As you may have noticed in the beginning, my laptop was not functioning at all, and therefore my paging will be different because I started five minutes later than you did. So I apologise for not saying that on my page 55.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you search for the wording -- let me just then make it relative and see how far it is from my present --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now in the middle of 57. So you should go approximately back two pages from the running transcript, where it is now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It's obviously inconvenient for Your Honour to have unsynchronised numbering, but may I say it's equally inconvenient for everybody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just read the part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have no problem. I'll read the whole of the answer: "Well, I have to say that his opinion was only a confirmation of what I thought."

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, one moment. I wonder if we could have the opportunity of simply finding the passage first. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Once -- it would be -- we suggest it will save time if we do simply -- if we are able to find the passage, then we can move very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could I just ask for the introductory phrase again to the passage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's page 61, line 1 according to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: On ours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At least on the registrar's.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, that's very helpful. Thank you. 61, line 1. 61, I think. 61?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 61, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. "When he said this to me I knew that he was referring to the highest organs of Republika Srpska, which had already been established and was already functioning as a real state."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "And the leadership of Serbia. So I presume that he referred to the highest-positioned leaders in Serbia at that moment."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So partly knowledge, at least claimed knowledge, and partly presumption. I think your question was whether the witness said that he knew or that he presumed, and I indicated to you, and that was the basis of my question, I made a clear distinction between the two, that part of his testimony was what he knew, as far as the reference is concerned, and partly that he presumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He knew about the organs, which is slightly more conceptual than individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not discuss it any further. Could you please tell us, Mr. Deronjic, now that the matter has been clarified, what made you to know that he was referring to the organs of the Republika Srpska, and what made you presume that he was referring to the Serbian high-level authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, let me try to explain this as best as I can. I myself was able to conclude during that period that the activities of the volunteers and the military on the ground were taking place according to a certain plan. I was able to see personally what the behaviour was of the state organs in Serbia during the process of the arming of the population, in particular, when the volunteers arrived in the area. I was personally present when this happened in Bajina Basta. The conduct of the local state organs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you. My first question: Is it on the basis of his words that you knew what he was referring to or that you presumed what he was referring to, or was it on the basis of knowledge outside, obtained outside of that conversation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said -- I cannot quote his exact words, but he said that there had been an agreement between the highest organs of Republika Srpska and those in Serbia with respect to the operations that were conducted in the area. So on the basis of that, I was able to assume that he was referring to the highest organs. Obviously, he was not referring to low-level organs. I was a low-level organ myself. But I was also personally able to conclude that this was part of a plan that had been agreed at the very highest level. Now, I do not have any specific piece of information which would confirm this, apart from what I could personally see on the 11th of May, when I reported what had happened in Glogova to the highest organs in Republika Srpska. And you know that I was not arrested, not even criticised, but was, quite the contrary, applauded for what had happened and for what I had done in Glogova, which confirmed to me that this was all part of a plan that had been mentioned by Goran Zekic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, let's continue, then, with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, are we going to go until 11.25 [sic]?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I had in mind. But if you would find this a more suitable moment, then we'll stop just a bit early and restart a bit earlier again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. I think this would be a suitable moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a 15 minutes' break until 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, please -- oh, we are not -- the witness is not in yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Deronjic. Mr. Harmon, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, did you come to any conclusions in respect of what you had seen occurring in other municipalities, adjacent municipalities, and what you saw occurring in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I came to the conclusion that this was organised and that, like I said, the top organs participated in the organisation of those activities in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, after you had a meeting with Mr. Zekic on the 5th -- 4th or 5th in the Hotel Fontana, did you have occasion to meet with Captain Reljic of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what occurred in that meeting with Captain Reljic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After talking with Mr. Zekic, I asked for the commander -- I looked for the commander of this unit in Bratunac, Mr. Reljic, and I wanted to talk to him about my thoughts about Glogova, which was in that location, and the idea to forcibly remove the population from that village 17 and from Bratunac. I talked to Mr. Reljic about this. I told him that those 18 were my thoughts about the development of the war in our area, and I 19 suggested that the actions should be carried out within the following few 20 days. He was quite restrained and he said that he would consult about this with his superiors and that we would reach an agreement on this. That was the essence of my meeting with Mr. Reljic. And I would just like to note that my relationship with him at that point was slightly better than when he had just arrived at Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And when you say: "I suggested that the actions should be carried out within the following few days," what actions were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I mentioned it already. I was thinking about the forcible transfer of the population from the village of Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, after you had this -- after you concluded your meeting with Captain Reljic, did you have a meeting with a man named Predrag Spasojevic

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who is Predrag Spasojevic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Predrag Spasojevic is a member of the state security services in Serbia. He appeared in Bratunac in late April. He showed me his ID, his membership with those units, and he said that he would be monitoring the events in Bratunac, that that would be his task there. That's what he told me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I just interrupt for one second? I'm trying to understand your testimony as good as I can; therefore, I have one additional question in respect of one of your answers. You said that your decision to start an action of forcible removal of the population of Glogova, it was, that you explained to Mr. Reljic what the developments of war in the area at that moment was. I understood this to be that these developments of the war in the area made you consider that it would be necessary or useful to forcibly transfer the population of Glogova. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the intention was to remove the population from Glogova. The remaining population in Bratunac and the surrounding settlements. Amongst other reasons, also because of the war and the events of the war in that region. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you explain that to me? I mean, what had happened in the war that made it necessary or useful to forcibly remove the population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In that period, there was armed fighting in the neighbouring municipalities. I'm primarily thinking of Zvornik and Srebrenica, because I was able to follow that directly, and also through people who were going to that area. They conveyed this information to me. Bratunac is in between those two municipalities. The events in Srebrenica of the 20th of April, when these volunteers were killed, led to open conflict. There was fighting in Srebrenica continually. There were also casualties in the town itself and in the neighbouring villages. Serbs and Muslims were being killed. Srebrenica is completely linked to the Bratunac municipality all along its territory, and because of the number of Muslims in that municipality, we were worried in Bratunac because of those numbers. And the moving out of the population from Bratunac, from Srebrenica, from Zvornik, was also one of the things we had to take into consideration. We were also able to see some attacks on some Serbian villages in Srebrenica. These are the villages of Gniona, Studenac, Bljeceva, which were torched, or parts of them were torched, and some Serbs were killed. I think ten Serbs were killed in those villages in that period. The war was getting more and more intense around Bratunac, and in Bratunac itself, it was impossible to completely control the situation, because there were people with weapons, both in Muslim and Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give me any indication? Because I do -- if I do understand you well, you say: Well, the war was developing. There were some volunteers were killed, volunteers that, from what I understood from your testimony, entered the area, killed people, robbed people, but were then -- some of them were killed. Could you give me a general impression of the development of war in terms of numbers of casualties. I mean, if you would have to give an impression of how many Serbs, approximately, were killed. Because you mentioned that some Serbs were killed; I think you mentioned the number of ten in a certain village. On a total, how many Muslims were killed? That's one question. And also, how many Muslim villages were taken over, compared to Serbian villages being attacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The number of casualties, up until 9th of May, is something that I don't know. I told you about these three villages about which I have information. In the town of Srebrenica itself, I know four or five local Serbs were killed in that period. And as far as I can recall, the number of Muslims who were killed in Srebrenica was about the same. We had some indirect information about this. People talked about it. I described the killings of five people in Bratunac, and this happened just when the volunteers entered the town. No Muslim village was occupied by Serbian forces in Bratunac or Srebrenica. This means that Goran Zekic, in Srebrenica, controlled the town and the institutions in the town, but had not taken any of the villages around -- surrounding the town. As far as Bratunac was concerned, the first action to occupy any of the Muslim villages took place on the 9th of May, and these are the events in Glogova. This is when we forcibly removed the population from Glogova. And I also said that three villages were attacked in that period by Muslim forces. These are the villages of Gniona, on the 6th of May; then Studenac. Some people were killed and some people were transferred. The villages were torched. And in Bljeceva, a part of it was attacked, inhabited by Serbs. It was a mixed-population village. Three people were killed, two woman and one man. I know their names and I have information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're talking about Serbian people or -- the three and the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three Serbs were killed in Bljeceva, two women and one man, an elderly man. His last name Jovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were any Muslims killed in that village that you said was a mixed village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if there were any Muslim casualties. It's possible, but I don't have information about that, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand from your answer that on the basis of a -- I would say a relatively low number of casualties in the surrounding villages and municipalities, Srebrenica, you said five, five, approximately, that you decided to forcibly remove the whole of the population in Glogova? Is that ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that one of the motives to move out the population was the development of the war around us. This is what I wish to say. And I also stated this in the factual basis. That the objective was to move out the population forcibly from Bratunac, from the town of Bratunac, its environs, and also from Glogova, primarily from Glogova, in order to implement complete control over the Bratunac municipality, in terms of carrying out the governing activities and the protection of that area. There were a lot of civilians in that region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, we were talking about Mr. Predrag Spasojevic, and you said who he was. He was from Serbian state security. And my question is: Mr. Deronjic, why did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that period, I had the opportunity to meet him several times. This is from the time he came to the Bratunac municipality and introduced himself to me. I noticed that he was the one who was carrying out these police tasks, that he often went to the police station in Bratunac and had contacts with those people. I knew that he was a member of certain units of the state security of Serbia. And I wanted to get some kind of signal from him about whether my decision to forcibly empty the Glogova village was a decision which will not run counter to the plans which his superiors had. And by that I'm thinking of the state security bosses in Serbia. These were the reasons why I spoke with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did you discuss your plan?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed our plan. And I would just like to add that he said that he believed and that he was sure that his bosses believed that my plan was all right and that it would secure some kind of military dominance in Bratunac, dominance by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What were your feelings after you left that conversation with Mr. Spasojevic? Were you more confident in your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I wanted to know that my further actions were not contrary to the plans of the Serbian side, including Serbia and Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thereafter, Mr. Deronjic, did you have another meeting with Captain Reljic from the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point we received an invitation to come to a meeting. I believe it was in the morning of the 7th that we were asked to come and look at the village of Glogova from a vantage point. So we went to the village of Magasici, where I was born.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Reljic and myself. I don't remember anyone else having been with us. So we went to Magasici, the village where I was born, located on high ground in the vicinity of Glogova, which can be plainly seen from Magasici. So we had a good look at it. He spent some time observing the village in some detail, and we returned to Bratunac with the agreement that the operation should take place within the several next days [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who was charged with actually planning the operational details of the attack?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't task anyone specifically. The military side of the plan was done by Mr. Reljic, by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, on the 8th of May, what happened to Goran Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Zekic was killed on the 8th of May, in an ambush which had been laid by Muslims in Potocari. His body was brought to Bratunac in the afternoon hours of that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What effect did Goran Zekic's death have on the Serbian population in Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think that it had consequences for the Serbian population in Srebrenica. On that day, in the hour of that day and during the evening hours, the entire population of -- Serbian population of Srebrenica left the town. My two sisters lived there, and they too left Srebrenica in the course of that night, together with their families. The population fled in the direction of Bratunac and Serbia, having completely abandoned the area. As regards the town of Bratunac, when the body of Goran Zekic was brought, a large number of people gathered - I cannot tell you the exact number, but I know that many of them had gathered in front of the town hall when the body of Goran Zekic was brought. I myself was present there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was the funeral for Goran Zekic planned?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, on the same day of his killing, in the evening of the 8th of May, did the crisis staff convene?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct. We met and held a session of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who attended that session of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That session of the crisis staff, apart from the members of the crisis staff, was attended -- I cannot remember the exact number of the members, maybe five or six, was attended by Mr. Reljic, representing the JNA unit, and Mr. Spasojevic, the man who was a member of the state security units from Serbia. Of course, there was also the chief of police and the Bratunac TO commander. The Territorial Defence of Bratunac had in the meantime been established as a separate institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was there anybody from the Kravica Territorial Defence attending that session?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of a unit of the Territorial Defence of Kravica, Jaso Nunic [phoen], who was soon to be killed, I think in the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What was the last name of the person you mentioned from Kravica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Raso Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, can you explain to the Judges what happened at that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting consisted of two parts. The first part was dedicated to the analysis of the events in Srebrenica and the killing of Goran Zekic, which of course came as a huge surprise, and it was indeed a tragic event, and we dedicated a lot of time to that. He was a prominent leader at the time. His family had been made aware of his killing, so his father appeared at the meeting as well. We were trying to arrange for the details of the funeral. We made plans for the following day. And during the second half of the session, we discussed the military situation, military activities, including the attack on Glogova. It was at that time that we decided that the forcible transfer of the population of Glogova should take place the next morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: During the course of that meeting, was there any discussion about burning Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We discussed that as well. We debated whether it was necessary to set the entire village or only a part of the village on fire. The discussion ended -- of course, some of the people were absolutely against it. I wish to point that out. And I suggested that some of the buildings in the village of Glogova should be set on fire as a warning. So it was my suggestion that part of the buildings should be set on fire but that the rest should not be touched, that is, that not the entire village was to be torched.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the conclusion of that meeting of the crisis staff, what decision was taken in respect of the attack on Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was decided that vehicles should get ready to come to the village of Glogova, depending on the course of the operation, and I refer to the lorries that were to transfer the entire population which we thought we would find in the village of Glogova to the municipality of Kladanj, the municipality which was under the control of the Muslims, and it was the nearest municipality to which we could send these people. It was also decided that, in case there should be no resistance, all villagers should be evacuated. In case of any resistance and fighting, which is something which we could not foresee, though the objective remained the same, this objective would have to be achieved through fighting. We couldn't, therefore, foresee whether there would be any fighting in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Glogova had been previously disarmed, according to your testimony; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: At the crisis staff meeting, did Captain Reljic say that he would -- he and his unit would participate in the operation against the village of Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted Mr. Reljic to provide us with a direct answer. Before each operation, each decision on an operation, I asked him whether he would take part with his JNA unit in the operation, and his answer was affirmative. He said yes, he would participate in the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What other units participated in the operation against Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Bratunac TO participated, together with the police, the Bratunac police, to the extent we had police officers at the station at that time. A number of volunteers, and also a certain number of residents of Srebrenica, because after the fall of Srebrenica into the hand of the Muslims, part of the unit moved to Bratunac, and they took part in the operation on Glogova. So those would be the units that participated in the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, after the conclusion of this meeting, did you and others go to the surrounding areas of Glogova and assume positions, military positions, around the village?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You said you and other members of the crisis staff. No. I went alone, together with the Territorial Defence unit, which, by the way, was also my unit, according to my war assignment. So it was together with them that I went to this tasking, the task being for this unit to interpose between Glogova and the Bratunac municipality, and a number of villages, Muslim villages, in the municipality of Srebrenica. I am referring to Potocari in particular. So it was between 11.00 and 12.00 p.m. that we deployed on the high grounds between Glogova and the remaining Muslim area of the Srebrenica municipality, and partly Bratunac municipalities as well, because Bljeceva, Cizmici, and other Muslim villages were behind our backs. Those villages also being part of the Bratunac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the crisis staff meeting the night of the 8th. And did you discuss any attacks on other Muslim settlements following the attack on Glogova; and if so, which Muslim settlements were targeted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We adopted a decision, under certain reservations, that should there be no fighting in Glogova, and if the operation ends without casualties, that we would continue with the operation of the forcible removal of the Muslim population in Bratunac, in particular, the Suha and Voljevica suburbs. We also agreed that these people should not be surrounded. There was no possibility to do that, but because of their number, they should be called upon through loudspeakers that they were to leave Bratunac and gather at specific locations in order to be evacuated from the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, let me take you back to the early morning hours of the 9th of May. Can you tell the Judges when the attack started, and can you describe the attack.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack started at 6.00 a.m., very early in the morning. Perhaps not exactly at 6.00, but it was in the early morning hours. I was on the high ground above the area, and I could observe the events. I could see the road from Bratunac and the approach of our force from Bratunac. As for the actual entry into the village, it preceded from the north, so far as I could tell. The village had already been surrounded by our TO units, and as far as I could see, the military was inside the village, with their APCs and a tank. It was then that the burning of certain buildings started, proceeding from the southern part of the village. So that was the beginning of the events in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, were you monitoring the events in Glogova from your vantage point?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I could observe the most part of the movements. I couldn't see the military with my naked eye; however, I was able to see the opening of fire and the torching of buildings. Very soon we could see thick smoke coming from various directions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you receive any information during the course of the morning about whether there was any resistance in the village?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received such information. The commander of the unit where I was, was Mr. Miloje Bozic, a reserve officer and one of the commanders in the TO. He had a Motorola, a communications device. And at one point I took it and wanted to hear the commanders of the detachment, to see if everything was all right in the village, because we could still hear the shooting going on in the village. But the information I received was that there was no resistance and that the operation was proceeding as planned, and that, for the time being, we had no casualties. That's what was reported to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you eventually leave your position and walk in the direction of the village of Glogova yourself, along with other members of your unit?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took a side road around the village of Glogova, walking in the direction of the west, to the west side of the village. I didn't enter the village, because this macadam dirt road goes around the village. We left with a group of soldiers, because we had been informed that the events had finished, that the population was being gathered in the centre of the village, and that we no longer had any role to play, that these people would be transported. On the way to Bratunac, I therefore passed by the village of Glogova. In the centre of the village I could see the presence of the military, the APCs and the tank were in the centre of the village. I saw the police and I saw the vehicles that were to take the population in the direction of Kladanj. One of them was leaving. There may have been others that I had not seen. I did not stay there. I proceeded directly to Bratunac to attend the funeral of Mr. Zekic, because we had agreed --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, while you descended into the village, did you personally authorise the burning of any Muslim homes; and if so, could you describe that to the Judges, please.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On two occasions I approved of the burning of some of the houses. When we got to the edge of the village, a number of troops entered four or five houses that were in the vicinity to check if anyone was in there, in order to ensure our safety, and they told us that the houses were empty. They wanted to know whether they should burn those houses, and I said yes. On the way to Kravica, I came across a TO unit from the village of Jezestica on an elevation there. I knew their commander and I ordered that several houses in the area should be set on fire, which they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, as a result of the action against the village of Glogova, the military action, at the conclusion of that action, were there any Muslims 8 left in the village? A. No. Now, I have to say that part of the population 9 had hid during the night. I know this for sure, because they had been 10 informed of our action. So a large number of people managed to hide, and in 11 the following days they came back to Glogova and in some later actions numerous Serbs were killed there , including Rasa Milosevic, who was killed in an ambush which was organised after this action. However, for the most part, the population was removed by us, and from what I know today, I know that about ten vehicles, including buses and lorries, left the area carrying the local population, including women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were a substantial number of the Muslim homes burned as a result of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were 65 Muslim villagers killed as a result of that operation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with your view. I never checked the number, but I have no reason to doubt it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What happened to the mosque in the village?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day, in the afternoon, I think that the mosque was blown up by explosives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, where did you go -- you started to tell us where you went on the 9th of May. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I returned to Bratunac immediately after the order that our role as a TO unit was finished in Glogova. I returned to the Fontana Hotel, to the funeral wake of Goran Zekic. I've already said that his family was already in Bratunac. Many people gathered. We said goodbye to Goran Zekic in front of the Fontana Hotel. He was taken to Ljubovija, in Serbia, where he was buried at the town cemetery, according to the wishes of his family. I was in the column going to Ljubovija and I attended the funeral services in church, and also I went to the graveyard where Mr. Zekic was buried. I attended the ceremony there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, following the attack on Glogova, can you tell the Judges what happened to the Muslim settlements of Suha and Voljevica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the morning, I noticed that the army and the police acted according to our agreement reached at the crisis staff, to continue with the evacuation of Suha and Voljevica from the town of Bratunac. I did not notice but I'm not saying that this is absolutely so, but I did not notice the TO taking part in this action. Mostly it was the police and the army who were calling people to come to the bus station in Bratunac or to the stadium. I don't know whether there was another location perhaps in Voljevica - I wasn't there - for the people to come to those locations and that they would be transported in the direction of Kladanj. This operation lasted the whole day. In the afternoon, I left Bratunac and went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, did the Muslim residents of Suha and Voljevica have a choice in the matter?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I did not take part in that. However, some people came to see me in the morning, having heard about this call for them to forcibly leave Bratunac. I have some statements, and I saw some statements also at the OTP. People came to me. I wasn't able to suggest anything to them. I even told one of those people that I would rather leave Bratunac myself also. I didn't notice anyone being arrested or escorted out of Bratunac. But because there were so many things going on, because of an atmosphere of fear and panic, a large number of people responded to this summons, and they gathered at these various locations in order to leave Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Deronjic, I just want to put this, what you characterise as an evacuation, in the proper perspective. On the night of the 8th of May, a decision was taken to attack Glogova, and if that was successful, then the forcible transfer of people from Suha and Voljevica would take place. My question really comes down to this: Did the Muslims in Suha and Voljevica have a choice? Could they have said: No. I wish to remain here. We want to stay in our community. We're happy here?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think that that was not a realistic option, and they did not have the opportunity of staying in Bratunac, and no one was there who would be able to guarantee their safety if they stayed in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you said that those people from those communities were supposed to assemble at a particular location or locations. Where were they supposed to assemble?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a brief remark. In the translation, it was said from those municipalities, but I think the translation should be from those settlements.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. All right. What I said was from those communities, but settlements is the same thing. Where was it specifically they were supposed to assemble?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the locations was the stadium in Bratunac; another location was on a plateau in front of the bus station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you learn, prior to going to Pale, that something was happening to the men?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received information that volunteers were at the stadium and that they were robbing those people first, and then that they had separated a group of men from the women and children. Mr. Rodoljub Djukanovic, the president of the Executive Board, and myself went there to see what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What did you see?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came close to the stadium, I was greeted by a group of these volunteers. They were waiting for me, and I could see on the right side of the stadium, along the wall, men lined up against that wall. I asked what this was all about, why these people were there, and I was told that there was an order from the army to detain those people in order to allegedly exchange them for captured Serbs in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I objected to that, and so did Mr. Djukanovic, but we provoked quite a strong reaction from those armed volunteers. On the way back, Djukanovic and I stopped at the police station, where we found the deputy chief, or the commander - I don't remember exactly who - his name was Luka Bogdanovic. We told him what was going on at the stadium, and we asked that he should try to do something together with the police. He said that all of his men were out in the field and that he would call the people to go to those places, and except for one or two police officers, he didn't have any personnel at the station. Shortly after that, I was called away to go to Pale. When I returned to the -- then I returned to the municipal building and then went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Why did you go to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell the Court exactly. I said that I was summoned to go, and I still think that I was summoned to Pale, but I cannot remember whether the summons was conveyed through the police or through the SDS. I went with the intention of attending a meeting. I think that's what I was told. I set off for Pale in a police car, escorted by one police officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Pale was the capital of the Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, did you attend a particular meeting in Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon. I attended the meeting. I came to the meeting. I concluded that the meeting was already in progress when I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Judges the physical layout of the room where this meeting took place.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my best recollection, it was a large room, a conference room in a building. I cannot remember what building it was any more. The meeting was attended by about 50 people from various municipalities. This is what I was able to conclude at that time. Mr. Mladic, Ratko Mladic, Mr. Radovan Karadzic, and Mr. Ostojic were there, perhaps some other people, but I didn't really pay attention. I am sure about these three, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you said 50 people attended this meeting. What positions do you recall those people held?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew some of the people. I cannot say that I knew all of them. I knew a few people there. They were mostly the presidents of municipal boards. And at the time, definitely, presidents of crisis staffs. Brano Grujic, for example, from Zvornik, was one of the people I knew. Some people I knew personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who were the other people you knew personally?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly today. I don't want to make a mistake. I did see Brano Grujic. I knew him. But I don't dare -- I knew some other people, such as the presidents of the municipal boards. I think that I saw people from Visegrad there. I think that I saw Mr. Stanic, that is, Miro Stanic, from Srbinje. But I'm not 100 per cent sure. I think they were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, where were Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Ostojic, and Ratko Mladic seated in relation to the other attendees at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First let me say that at the entrance to this conference room, as far as I can remember, there was a table to the right, at which they sat. So they were facing this group. They were chairing the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say Mr. Ostojic, is that Mr. Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you've identified in your previous testimony his role in the SDS. Now, in respect of the locations of Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Ostojic, and Ratko Mladic, were there any maps in the room?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the wall behind them, there was a map. I think that it was a map of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but I didn't really pay much attention whether perhaps it was a map of Yugoslavia. In any case, the topic of the meeting was Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And what was the -- from your observations, once you arrived at that meeting, what did it appear to you was the purpose of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just give you my impression, which was confirmed when I addressed the meeting, when I submitted my report, the point of the meeting was for the local people to submit reports, either the presidents of the municipal boards or the presidents of the crisis staffs. These were the key figures out in the field, and they were reporting about the military situation in the field. I was at the meeting for a very brief time. I requested to submit my report as soon as possible, not waiting for my turn, because of the seriousness of the situation in Bratunac and because I needed to return to Bratunac by the evening. It was well known that the situation was very risky. The driver accompanied me to the meeting. His name was Vidoje Radojevic. He was a police officer and my driver. We sat next to each other, and I was given the opportunity to submit my report out of order, or perhaps I was submitting my report when my turn came.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What report --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About the situation in the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What specifically did you report to Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Ostojic, and Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Briefly - and I didn't speak for long - I informed the leadership at the meeting about the situation, the events in Glogova. I said that the day before, the 9th of May, we carried out the forcible transfer of the population from Glogova, that the village was torched, most of the village was torched, and that all the inhabitants of the village who happened to be there when we came were evacuated in the direction of Kladanj. I also told them, as far as I can recall, that the operation was continuing in Bratunac and that Muslims were being asked to leave the area of the Bratunac town and the surrounding settlements by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Deronjic, what was the response of the people in attendance at that meeting to your report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in my prior testimony. After I finished my testimony, or, actually, my report, I received a round of applause from the people who were sitting in the conference room. I am not counting the people who were presiding over the meeting, but the people who were sitting in the conference room gave me a round of applause.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did any of the people who were presiding over the meeting make any remarks after you concluded your report?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic was the first to ask me to point out on the map where the village of Glogova was. That was the first time I saw Mr. Mladic. He was interested in the military units and who was commanding them in Bratunac, so I told him what I knew. Then Mr. Ostojic added a sentence to the effect that now that municipality, the municipality of Bratunac, can be painted blue. That was the comment that he made at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, looking at the clock --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm looking at it very carefully, Your Honour, and I have one or two more questions and I will finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because I've started already by having a short break, a couple of minutes from the interpreters. But if one or two minutes would do, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Were the maps that were behind Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Mladic, and Mr. Karadzic coloured with various colours and what did those colours designate?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The colours represented the ethnic composition in the field. The green colour marked the municipalities or the settlements. I'm not sure. I didn't really pay that one attention [as interpreted]. But you could see that some areas of the map were coloured green, some were blue. I don't know how the Croats were represented on the map. There weren't too many of them in this region, so I didn't notice that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What population group was represented by green, and what population group was represented by blue?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The green represented Muslims, and the blue represented the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions at this point. Thank you. I will be brief in my remaining areas of examination with Mr. Deronjic the next time he appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And what means "brief"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour, I can finish in probably 30 minutes or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, may I ask Mr. Deronjic to be escorted out of the courtroom. I know, Mr. Usher, it's not entirely in your hands, but ... Mr. Deronjic, we'll -- presumably on Wednesday, we'll continue. That would be Wednesday afternoon. A final decision has not been taken by the Chamber yet whether we continue tomorrow or Wednesday, but Wednesday is more likely. And may I again instruct you not to speak with anyone, nor parties, nor other detained parties, nor other persons not detained, to speak about your testimony given and still to be given. Then you may leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I indicated already that it was more likely that we would continue on Wednesday, given the fact, although a bit of a surprising fact for the Chamber, that the Prosecution says that it's not ready. And let me be quite clear that one day being ready and the other day not being ready any more needs at least some explanation, the Chamber has not received yet, and we don't -- can't spend time on it now, but in general terms, this change of position by the Prosecution perhaps should have been announced prior to telling this Chamber in Court. But it seems to be a matter of fact. The Chamber does agree with the Defence that it's not practical to ask Mr. Deronjic to come in tomorrow for half an hour. That means that Mr. Krajisnik should also be transported for this half an hour to the courtroom. That's not a very practical way of proceeding. Therefore, under the conditions that the parties agree later this afternoon on what their time path would be, that if the Chamber could expect such a common time path to be presented later this afternoon - it should not be very elaborated, but just to state that they -- and I do understand that the parties have discussed the matter already - that we would then continue on Wednesday, in the afternoon, at a quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom II -- III. Courtroom III. I correct myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I just say, Your Honour, that we gave what we -- is a fairly simple proposed timetable. Actually, we gave that at the beginning of the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not going to take any more time from the interpreters. I do understand that you gave something to the Prosecution. We'll see this afternoon whether the Prosecution agrees. If so, it's quite simple. If not, we'll let the parties know what our decision will be. But if we receive something acceptable for the Chamber - and it would be difficult to offer something not acceptable. I add that - then we'll continue next Wednesday, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: sine die. 23 24 25
